title: yunta event
description: One event of a run's log: the envelope and the payload of its `kind`, side by side in one object

AdapterId.description: An adapter id: a letter followed by letters, digits, `_` or `-`

target.description:
What the tool acted on. Absent for a message that is not a tool
call, and for a log written before the engine recorded it.

AgentName.description: An agent name: printable ASCII without whitespace

fence.description:
How much of this session the adapter's fence covered — derived
from what it built, never declared. Absent when it built none.
The level travels once, in `capabilities.fence`.

model.description:
The model the CLI reported for the session; absent when it
reported none.

ArtifactAcceptedPayload.description:
One artifact the run holds: what it is, the bytes it is made of, and
how the run came by it.

This is what makes an artifact a fact of the log rather than a file
somebody may have replaced: the identity says which artifact, the
hash says which content, and the envelope's `node_id` says who
produced it — absent for what a run acquires without a node of its
own (a `document` input, a mount, a promotion).

The field is named `artifact`, not `kind`, for the reason
[`ArtifactWrittenPayload::artifact_kind`] gives: the event
envelope's own internally-tagged discriminant already claims `kind`
in the serialized JSON, and a colliding field name silently corrupts
the payload.

ArtifactFailure.description:
Why one declared artifact did not close.

The variants answer the one question that decides what is worth
doing next: rewriting the content reaches [`Content`](Self::Content),
nothing this node writes reaches [`File`](Self::File) or
[`Undelivered`](Self::Undelivered), and nothing this run does at all
reaches [`Unheld`](Self::Unheld), because the artifact is another
run's to produce.

oneOf.description: The file itself. No rewrite of its content reaches this.

Declared by a node the run's own log answers for, and never
handed over: the node ended without the document it owes.

No path, for the same reason [`Unheld`](Self::Unheld) has none.
Such a document never is a file on its way in — a session hands
it over through its submission tool, the engine derives it from
what the node posted — so the close opened nothing and there is
no file to name.

artifact.description:
What the node owes: the identity, which is what a log
answers by.

node.description: The node that declared it and ended owing it.

oneOf.description: The file is there and its content is not what its kind declares.

Declared here and held by no run that could hand it over: the
run that owes it — a `kind: workflow` node's child, or the run a
mount names as its source — answers with nothing under this
identity.

A node of composition writes no file, so there is nothing on
disk to be missing and nothing this run does reaches the
artifact: producing it is another run's to do.

artifact.description:
What the run was asked for: the identity, which is what a
log answers by.

producer.description:
The node of that run the artifact was asked of, when the
reference names one. `None` when the question is about the
run as a whole, which is what a `kind: workflow` node asks
of its child.

run.description:
The run that was asked and holds none of it — where a reader
goes to look.

ArtifactId.description:
What an artifact is, which is what a reader asks for it by.

An artifact the engine interprets is identified by its kind: a run
holds one tasks document, whoever produced it, so a reader asks for
the kind and never needs to know the file name its workflow chose.
One the engine only carries is identified by the name the workflow
declared, which is the only thing that distinguishes it from any
other opaque artifact.

ArtifactKind.description:
A document the engine reads and validates, as opposed to an artifact
it only checks for existence. The kind fixes the document's shape, so
it is what every door — the workflow's own `kind:`, `yunta schema`,
the `document_shape` tool, a failed read's report — names it by.

ArtifactOrigin.description:
Where an artifact came from, as the log spells it: the recorded
origins and `legacy` are one tagged set on the wire, while in Rust a
fresh acceptance can only name a [`RecordedOrigin`]. `serde` moves
between the two here, so the type the engine holds is not shaped by
the file it is written to.

ArtifactSubmittedPayload.description:
What a session offered as a whole document, and what the engine
answered.

artifact_kind.description:
Named `artifact_kind`, not `kind`, for the reason
[`ArtifactWrittenPayload`] gives: the envelope's own tag already
claims `kind` in the serialized JSON.

The artifact's declared `kind:` when it has one — what
lets `derive()` recognize a `questions` artifact without reading
any file (state comes from events alone). `None` for opaque
artifacts and for logs written before the field existed (tolerant
reader). Named `artifact_kind`, not `kind`: the event
envelope's own internally-tagged discriminant already claims
`kind` in the serialized JSON, and a colliding field name
silently corrupts the payload.

BaselineCapturedPayload.description:
What the suite a run's lineage declared did on the tree the run
opens on, and whose measurement it is.

origin.description:
Whose measurement this is. A log written before the field reads
[`BaselineOrigin::Measured`], which is what such a log meant.

BaselineOrigin.description:
Who took the measurement a run holds: this run, or the root of the
lineage it was born into.

A lineage measures once. A run born of another — a `kind: workflow`
child, a promotion successor — is born holding the root's
measurement, so every comparison anywhere in the lineage answers the
same question: what worked before the invocation started.

oneOf.description: This run ran the suite itself, on its first wake.

The run was born holding it; `run` is the root that measured,
never the parent it was handed down through.

BaselineResults.description:
What the suite reported: the code it exited with, and the tail a
reader sees without opening what the measuring run kept.

Capabilities.description:
An adapter's declared capabilities. Constant for the
lifetime of the adapter — the engine consults this before asking
for anything, and never emulates what is not declared.

Lives in `yunta-core` rather than `yunta-adapters` because it is also
the shape of `agent_session_opened`'s `capabilities` field;
both the event log and the `Adapter` trait
share this one definition instead of duplicating it.

custom_agents.description:
Supports the CLI's own named agents, selectable via the portable
`agent:` field.

fence.description:
What this adapter can build to keep a session's writes inside
its fence. `None` means nothing: the post-check diff is the only
thing that catches a write outside the scope. A log written
before the fence existed carries `edit_hooks` instead, which this
field's `default` reads as `None`.

network_isolation.description:
Can confine a session's process to no network access, enforcing a
node's `network: false`. Declarative policy is never an OS sandbox
Yunta core promises (D105): where this is absent, a node's
`network: false` degrades with `capability_degraded` — recorded for
policy and audit, never enforced.

resume_session.description: Can resume a previous conversation via `resume()`.

run_tools.description: Can connect to Yunta's per-run MCP server as a client.

skills.description:
Can mount skill directories (`SessionRequest.skills`) by the
CLI's native mechanism. A skill is added instruction,
never correctness: absence degrades with `capability_degraded`,
never a fatal error.

usage_reporting.description: Emits trustworthy token usage in the stream.

Capability.description:
One capability an adapter can declare: the closed set of
[`Capabilities`] fields, spelled the way `capability_degraded` records
them (`resume_session`, `run_tools`, …). The engine names the
capability it consulted with this type, so a degradation can never
cite a capability no adapter has.

capability.description: The capability the engine consulted and the adapter does not declare.

ChildRunCreatedPayload.description: The parent's `kind: workflow` node is the envelope's own `node_id`.

tokens.description:
The child run's whole derived spend at its close — a child
run's usage always aggregates up into its parent, so replay adds
it to the parent's own total. That means a promotion *chain*'s
every member counts exactly once, resumes included, and the
parent node's own `node_finished` carries no child tokens
(they'd double-count). Additive: events logged before this field
existed parse as zero.

CommitSha.description: A commit sha: 7 to 64 lowercase hex digits: a git object id, abbreviated or full

ContentHash.description: A content hash: 64 lowercase hex digits, the SHA-256 of the content

segment_hashes.description:
Keys are `"stable" | "run-stable" | "volatile"` (the fixed
stability classes) — kept as plain strings rather than an enum key
to sidestep serde's map-key-as-enum ceremony for no real benefit.

task_id.description:
`Some` when this assembly built one *task's* brief inside a loop
node — the same task-vs-node convention
`ScopeCheckedPayload.task_id` already follows. `None` for a
node-level assembly (a `prompt` node's own context). Additive:
events logged before this field existed parse with `None`.

ContextSourceRef.description:
One resolved `ContextSource` reference in `context_assembled.sources`.
`kind` stays a plain string — the engine fixes the *set* of
builtin source kinds (`files | command | artifact | run-events |
tasks | knowledge | node-output`, `mcp` among them) but never closes
it into an enum, since a pack can add its own sources without
this type needing to change. `content_hash` is what makes every
resolution's event carry a verifiable hash — the hash of exactly
the bytes the run stored under `objects/<content_hash>` for this
source, so replay can name precisely what a session saw without
re-running anything.

absent.description:
The optional `files:` paths this source did not find (D186): the
session got a marker in each one's place, and the hash above
covers that marker. Empty — and absent from the wire — for every
source that found all it read.

Coverage.description:
How much of a session the fence actually covered, derived from what
the adapter could build — never declared.

Criterion.description:
A tasks document criterion, frozen into `task_registered` — the same shape
the tasks parser produces.

duration_ms.description:
Wall-clock milliseconds this execution took — the datum
the learned criterion ordering feeds on. `None` for a `reused: true`
result (nothing ran) and for events logged before this field
existed (additive, tolerant reader).

Decider.description: `decided_by`: `rule | person` plus an identifier for the latter.

Diagnostic.description: One thing that is wrong with a document.

oneOf.description: The document as a whole, as opposed to an entry inside it.

A criterion names the task it belongs to, so a reader always has
somewhere to look — including when that task's own id is what
could not be read.

A node of a workflow, for a rule about the graph the file
declares.

The document does not parse into its kind: an unknown key, a
value of the wrong type, an id that is not one. `path` locates
the offending value from the document's root (`tasks[1].scope`),
and is empty when the root itself is the problem; `message` is
what the deserializer said about that value, which names the key
and what it expected.

A rule the document broke once it was readable — the tasks document's own
registration rules and their siblings. `code` is what a receipt
counts; `detail` is the clause a reader acts on.

DocumentKind.description:
What kind of document a report is about.

Every document this system reads is held to a shape and to rules,
and reports what it found the same way — so a workflow that breaks
its own rules reaches a reader in the shape a tasks document already
does. The two are separate arms because they are read at different
moments by different doors: a workflow before any run, an artifact
at a node's close.

anyOf.description: The workflow file a run is created from.
A document a node produces and the engine reads.

DocumentRef.description:
Which document a report is about: the kind that fixes its shape, and
where a reader opens it.

A document always has a kind. An artifact the engine never
interprets has no shape to demand and therefore no content to report
on; what can go wrong with one is a [`FileProblem`] instead. An
artifact another run owes has no document at all, and names none.

path.description: As a reader would type it to open the file.

Envelope.description:
The wire shape's envelope fields. Kept apart from [`StoredEvent`] so
the body can be flattened beside them by hand: serde's own
`flatten` cannot fall back to an unknown kind.

schema_version.description:
Present only for an unknown kind, whose version has no other
place to live on the wire; a known kind's version is its own.

EventPayload.description: All event kinds, internally tagged by `kind`.

Evidence.description:
The facts behind an escalation's summary, attached by the engine
straight from the log.

The pair is the point: the summary is a *claim* about what happened
and this is the *record* it is audited against, so neither one
repeats the other. A producer that writes the cause into both leaves
every surface printing it twice, under a heading that promised
something new.

Untagged, with `Prose` last: a payload carrying a list reads as
[`Evidence::Facts`], and a log written before evidence was data
carries one string and reads back as [`Evidence::Prose`], which
renders as the single unlabelled fact it always was. That tolerance
is the rule for what is persisted and versioned, and it is why no
reader needs to know which version wrote the line it is looking at.

anyOf.description:
What this binary writes: the labelled facts, in the order a
reader meets them.

One string, as an older log recorded it. Only reading produces
this; nothing in this workspace writes one.

Fact.description:
One fact the engine read off the log: the label a reader scans for,
and the value under it.

The label is optional because not every fact needs one. A cause like
`exit 1` or a sentence like `no forge reachable from this machine`
already names itself, and putting a word in front of it would add
reading without adding meaning; a bare number like `400` says
nothing until `limits.max_tokens_per_run` is in front of it. A fact
that carries a label states it here rather than writing it into the
value, so every surface sets the two apart the same way.

FenceLevel.description:
What an adapter can build to keep a session's writes inside its
fence. Three levels, because three is what the market has: nothing;
a judgement before each file-tool call; or a filesystem sandbox the
process itself runs under.

FileProblem.description:
What is wrong with the file, before anything inside it is read.

Each renders as the rest of the sentence "the document ...", because
there is no entry inside to blame and pointing at one would be an
invention.

oneOf.description: Declared by a node and never produced.
Produced with no content.

Past `limits.max_artifact_bytes`. Both numbers are on the table,
because a runaway artifact is a fact about the run and a
truncation would hide it.
Exists, and the filesystem refused it.

FindingId.description: A finding id: not empty and without control characters

FindingOperation.description: Which of the three a refused call was making.

FindingPostedPayload.description:
The finding's author is the envelope's own `node_id` — not repeated
here.

FindingRefusedPayload.description:
A finding a session offered and the engine did not take, with every
problem named. The accepted cases are the three events above; this is
what a session was told instead, kept so the rate a run gets findings
wrong is a fact about the run rather than something only the session
saw.

id.description: The id the call named, when it named one that parses.

FindingSeverity.description:
`severity`: `blocking | major | minor | note` — confirmed against the
`kind: findings` schema, not inferred.

FindingUpdatedPayload.description:
The node's finding, in its new state — a whole replacement, never a
merge: a field absent from an update is absent from the finding.

FindingWithdrawnPayload.description:
The node's finding `id` no longer stands, and why — in the words of
whoever took it back.

GateOption.description:
One choice in a gate's escalation: `id` is what
`GateResolvedPayload.chosen_option` names back, `label` is the
human-facing text, `tradeoff` is mandatory — any option that expands
scope of work must declare what it trades off, and no variant of
this type can omit it.

GateResolvedPayload.description:
How a gate's escalation was settled. On the wire this is one flat
object of four optional fields, and the fields present spell the
shape: an option with its responder is a human's `Chosen`; a
responder with a commit id is the forge's `Approved`; a responder
alone is `ChangesRequested`; nothing at all is `Closed`. Reading
decides the shape once, here, so every reader matches on it instead
of inferring it from which field is set. A combination no shape
names reads as `Unrecognized` and writes back verbatim: a newer
writer may mean something by it, and the export loses nothing.

approved_sha.description:
The commit the forge's approval covers: what a later drift check
compares against the pull request's current head to decide
whether the approval still holds.

chosen_option.description: The option a human chose from the menu.

free_text.description: Free-form context a human gave alongside the choice.

resolved_by.description:
Who decided: the human who chose, or the reviewer or merger the
forge reports.

evidence.description:
The record `summary` is audited against, attached by the engine
straight from the log.

external_ref.description:
The forge's own handle for this gate — a PR URL,
today — `None` for the internal escalation case (exhausted
re-routes) this payload already covered before external
gates existed. Round-trips the forge's `PublishedGate` through
the log so a later `poll` (from a completely different process
waking up to check on the gate) knows what to poll without
re-publishing.

summary.description:
The claim: what happened, in the words of whoever escalated.
It ends where the record begins — a summary that quotes what
`evidence` holds leaves every surface printing it twice.

InputName.description: An input name: a letter followed by letters, digits, `_` or `-`

Location.description: where a finding is: a path relative to the work, with its lines when they are known (`src/lib.rs`, `src/lib.rs:10`, `src/lib.rs:10-14`), or one relative to the run's own directory under the `run:` prefix (`run:objects`). Never absolute

ModeName.description: A mode name: a letter followed by letters, digits, `_` or `-`

ModelName.description: A model name: printable ASCII without whitespace

Named.description:
One entry of a document: by name when its id parsed, by position
when the id is the thing that could not be read.

The pair is one concept, so it is one type. Spelled as two loose
fields, the half that is easiest to forget is the position, and a
position that goes missing does not read as absent — it reads as
zero, and names the first entry with confidence.

Named2.description:
One entry of a document: by name when its id parsed, by position
when the id is the thing that could not be read.

The pair is one concept, so it is one type. Spelled as two loose
fields, the half that is easiest to forget is the position, and a
position that goes missing does not read as absent — it reads as
zero, and names the first entry with confidence.

Named3.description:
One entry of a document: by name when its id parsed, by position
when the id is the thing that could not be read.

The pair is one concept, so it is one type. Spelled as two loose
fields, the half that is easiest to forget is the position, and a
position that goes missing does not read as absent — it reads as
zero, and names the first entry with confidence.

Named4.description:
One entry of a document: by name when its id parsed, by position
when the id is the thing that could not be read.

The pair is one concept, so it is one type. Spelled as two loose
fields, the half that is easiest to forget is the position, and a
position that goes missing does not read as absent — it reads as
zero, and names the first entry with confidence.

NodeFailedPayload.description:
Why a node failed.

Untagged, with `Message` last: a payload carrying `artifacts:` reads
as [`Failure::Artifacts`], one carrying `died:` as
[`Failure::SessionDied`], and a log written before failures were
data carries `outcome:` alone and reads back as
[`Failure::Message`]. That tolerance is the rule for what is
persisted and versioned, and it is why no reader needs to know which
version wrote the line it is looking at.

retryable.description:
Whether this node will be attempted again. Set by whoever owns
the budget, so a failure that nothing will retry is never
recorded as retryable.

anyOf.description:
Declared artifacts that did not close, each saying what went
wrong with it: the file, the content of the document, or the run
that owes the artifact and holds none of it.

The session the node was working in ended without a terminal
event, and how its process went.
A failure the engine states in one sentence.

NodeId.description: A node id: a letter followed by letters, digits, `_` or `-`; a fan-out sibling adds `@` and its runner's name

NodeReroutedPayload.description:
`from_node` is the envelope's own `node_id` (the node that failed) —
only the re-route's destination is extra information.

attempt.description:
The retry count against the cap — present only for an
`on_failure` reroute, absent for a gate's routing choice, which
is not a retry and has no cap to count against.

origin.description:
Which mechanism rerouted. Old logs, written before the
distinction existed, carry no field and read as `OnFailure`.

from_tree.description:
The tree this attempt starts from — what its own diff is judged
against when it closes, so a node answers for what it changed and
not for what the run's worktree already held.

Absent in a log written before the audit had a recorded starting
point, and read then as the run's own base: the tolerance every
persisted field here gives a reader older than its writer.

OnInterrupt.description: A node's crash-recovery policy — the full triple of options.

oneOf.description:
Continue the same agent conversation — the
`session_id` the log recorded (`agent_session_opened`) is
handed back to the adapter's `resume`. Only `kind: prompt` opens
a node-scoped session, so `check` refuses the explicit
declaration anywhere else; an adapter without the
`resume_session` capability — or a crash before any session
opened — degrades to `restart_node` with an explicit
`capability_degraded` event, never silently. As a *config default*
(`defaults.on_interrupt`) it applies where a session exists;
kinds without one (bash/check/…, and a loop's per-task sessions)
restart, which is the only meaning the policy can have there.

OptionId.description: An option id: a letter followed by letters, digits, `_` or `-`

evidence.description:
The record `reason` is built from, kept apart so a surface can
show it under its own heading.

reason.description:
Why the run promoted, on one line — the claim and the facts
behind it, since this is the only field a reader of the event
itself gets.

QuestionId.description: A question id: a letter followed by letters, digits, `_` or `-`

QuestionsAskedPayload.description:
A node handed its questions over and closed on them: what it asked
from, which ids await an answer, and what the session that asked
spent.

The pair of [`QuestionsAnsweredPayload`]. Between the two the node
waits, and the `node_finished` its close deferred lands after the
answer — so a node that asked is never mistaken for one that failed,
and a log that holds a questions document is never mistaken for a
node that is waiting on it.

questions.description:
The ids awaiting an answer. Never empty: a node with nothing to
ask finishes in the same close instead of waiting.

questions_hash.description:
The questions document the node handed over: what the answers
answer, and what the round re-reads before putting them to
anyone.

tokens_used.description:
What the session that asked spent. The attempt's accounting
closes here, so the `node_finished` after the answer carries
none and no surface counts the session twice while it waits.

Report.description:
Every problem one document has, reported together.

Collecting them is not a convenience: a reader who corrects one
problem per round pays a round per problem, and a writer who hears
one rule at a time rewrites the document once per rule.

RerouteOrigin.description:
What caused a `node_rerouted`. The two mechanisms differ in kind: an
`on_failure` reroute is a bounded retry (it carries counters); a
gate's `on:` choice is a routing decision (it carries none).

Responder.description: A responder: not empty and without control characters

RuleCode.description:
The stable name of a rule that only holds across a whole
document.

Exhaustive, so a rule cannot be minted by typing a new string,
and countable, so a receipt reports what a run keeps getting
wrong without reading prose. A code says which rule broke and
nothing about which document it broke in: `DuplicateId` is one
rule asked of tasks documents, findings and questions alike, and what
separates the three is the
[`ArtifactKind`](crate::ArtifactKind) on the report carrying
it. Counting by code alone conflates them; counting by kind
and code does not.

Every variant belongs to some document's
[`RULES`](crate::shape::Document::RULES), so a rule the engine
enforces is a rule the writer was told about before writing.

oneOf.description: A second entry already carries this id.

Every criterion is a guard, so nothing in the task proves work
happened.
`depends_on` names a task nobody declared.
Two independent tasks reach for the same files.
An update or a withdrawal names a finding this node never posted.

A withdrawn id is final — it is not posted, updated or withdrawn
again.
A withdrawal does not say why.
`answer_type` is `choice` and `values` is empty.
A `required` question has no answer.
An answer's value is not what its question's `answer_type` allows.

A `mode` leaves out a node the workflow cannot run without, or a
node a node it includes reroutes to.

RunId.description: A run id: one path segment: printable ASCII without whitespace, `/` or `\`, and not `.` or `..`

policies.description:
Every node the log left running with no terminal event, and the
`on_interrupt` it resolved to: its own, or the config's default.

RunToolFailedPayload.description: One failed call to a tool this binary serves on `yunta-run`.

RunToolFailureCause.description: The closed reason a run tool call failed, without adapter error text.

RunnerCandidate.description: One binding candidate for a role in `runners:`.

RunnerName.description: A runner name: a letter followed by letters, digits, `_` or `-`

RunnerResolvedPayload.description:
`runner` names the `runners:` entry the node resolved through. The
reader also accepts `role`, the field's former name, so a log written
under it still replays.

SchemaRange.description: a schema range: whitespace-separated comparators (`>=`, `<=`, `>`, `<`, `=`) over whole schema majors, e.g. `>=1 <2`

paths.description:
The exact paths this grant authorized — self-contained
audit, and what a later attempt's effective scope derives from
the log, instead of re-pairing the grant with the
`requested` event that preceded it. `default` for logs written
before the field existed (tolerant reader).

ScopeExpansionMode.description:
How a loop node treats an agent's request to widen its scope.
Default `Deny`: a node that omits `scope_expansion:` entirely gets
the same behavior as one that declares it with no `mode:` — no
expansions, every request becomes a finding without interrupting.

ScopeGlob.description: a scope glob: a path pattern where `*` stays within one directory and `**` recurses

Seq.description: A position in a run's log: a positive number

SessionDeath.description:
A session that ended without ever reporting a terminal event: whose
it was, and how its process went, when it had one of its own.

SessionEnd.description:
How the process ended: the status it exited with, or the signal that
ended it.

A closed union rather than two optionals, so a process that says
neither is not representable. A stored `type` this build does not
know reads back as [`SessionEnd::Unknown`] — the tolerance everything
persisted here gives a reader older than its writer.

SessionExit.description:
What a process left behind: how it ended, and the last lines it wrote
to stderr, redacted of every value its environment carried.

SessionId.description: A session id: not empty and without control characters

SubmissionOutcome.description:
Accepted, and the file the engine wrote from it; or refused, and
every problem the document has.

TaskId.description: A task id: a letter followed by letters, digits, `_` or `-`

caused_by.description: `seq` of the event that justifies this transition.

commit.description:
Where the task's work landed, on a `done` and nowhere else: the
commit the run's tree carried after integrating it. What makes a
`done` answerable by another run — a tree either descends from
this commit or does not have the work.

TerminalState.description:
Exact variant names are provisional; a `cancel` command
exists, so `Cancelled` is included alongside the obvious two.

oneOf.description:
The run closed because its own gate accepted promotion
to a later-declared mode — never because the work itself failed
or was cancelled.

ToolTarget.description:
What a tool call acted on, as the log may carry it.

A tool's argument is the session's own text: a path, a shell command,
a URL. Some of it names the repository, which a reader needs; some of
it is whatever the session typed, which may be anything at all,
including a secret. So the log carries two things and they are not
the same thing: `display` is what a reader may be shown and is only
ever present for a value the engine itself can vouch for, and
`digest` is what identifies the target — the whole hash, so two
targets never share one. `abbreviated()` is how a hash is shown,
never how it is stored.

digest.description: What identifies the target, whether or not it can be shown.

display.description:
The target as a reader may see it. Absent whenever the value is
the session's own text.

TreeId.description: A tree id: 7 to 64 lowercase hex digits: a git object id, abbreviated or full

WriteRefusedPayload.description: A write the fence refused before it happened.
